title: Lateral Femoral Cutaneous Nerve Block (LFCN) in ACL Reconstruction With MacFL-type Lateral Tenodesis
official: Lateral Femoral Cutaneous Nerve Block (LFCN) in ACL Reconstruction With MacFL-type Lateral Tenodesis
summary:
The goal of this randomized clinical trial is to evaluate whether adding an ultrasound-guided lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN) block to a standard regional analgesia protocol improves postoperative recovery in patients undergoing anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction combined with MacIntosh-type lateral extra-articular tenodesis.

The main question the study aims to answer is whether adding an LFCN block to an adductor canal block (ACB) and an iPACK block improves the quality of postoperative recovery, as measured by the Quality of Recovery-15 (QoR-15) score at 24 hours after surgery.

The study will also assess:

* Preservation of quadriceps function, assessed by the ability to perform a straight leg raise (SLR).
* Postoperative pain at the lateral thigh graft harvest site and knee, at rest and during mobilization.
* Cumulative oral opioid consumption during the first 48 hours after surgery.
* Incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV).
* Time to first postoperative ambulation.
* Patient satisfaction with analgesic management.

Adverse events and complications related to regional anesthesia, including sensory disturbances, hematoma, infection, and signs of local anesthetic systemic toxicity.

Participants will be randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to one of two treatment groups. All participants will undergo ACL reconstruction combined with MacIntosh-type lateral extra-articular tenodesis and will receive an ACB and an iPACK block. Participants in the experimental group will additionally receive an ultrasound-guided LFCN block.

Postoperative assessments will include QoR-15, pain scores, opioid consumption, PONV, quadriceps function, ambulation, patient satisfaction, and safety assessments during the first 48 hours after surgery and at 1 month. The primary outcome will compare the QoR-15 score at 24 hours between the two groups, with an 8-point difference considered clinically meaningful.
